content: When comparing ad valorem taxation (AV) to specific taxation (SP), the amount of tax revenue generated depends on the type of taxation applied. Globally, various methods of alcohol excise taxation are employed, including uniform tax methods such as specific taxation, ad valorem taxation, and unitary taxation, as well as combination tax methods like mixed specific and ad valorem taxation or ad valorem taxation with a specific floor. Each of these methods has unique attributes and may be suitable for different contexts and alcohol control objectives depending on the country. Governments should consider three primary goals when selecting an alcohol excise taxation model: (1) generating tax revenue, (2) controlling alcohol consumption and addressing public health issues caused by alcohol, and (3) preventing the initiation of drinking, particularly in countries with high rates of lifetime abstention. Specific taxation may be more appropriate for high-income countries with a high prevalence of drinkers, as it encourages the consumption of beverages with lower alcohol content, thereby reducing overall alcohol consumption. On the other hand, mixed specific and ad valorem taxation (MSA) or ad valorem taxation with a specific floor (ASF) may be more suitable for lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), as these methods promote the consumption of beverages with medium alcohol content, which can reduce heavy drinking and prevent youth from initiating alcohol consumption. Governments may also implement minimum pricing measures to address problems associated with the availability of cheap alcoholic beverages. Two indicators are commonly used to assess the extent of a tax rate: the tax due as a percentage of the retail price (TPP) and the tax due per unit of ethanol (TPU). TPP is superior for measuring tax incidence, which reflects the tax burden on income distribution, while TPU is better for assessing the tax burden on each unit of ethanol. Both indicators should be used when comparing alcohol excise tax rates across countries. The 2012 Global Survey on Alcohol and Health (GSAH), conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO), collected data on alcohol consumption and control policies from member states. This survey provided a unique opportunity to study global alcohol taxation and pricing policies. The results, published in the Global Status Report on Alcohol and Health (2014), included information on the types of excise taxes applied to various alcoholic beverages and the amount of tax collected. However, previous publications based on GSAH data did not report on taxation systems but instead focused on topics such as legal drinking age, drink-driving laws, and whether excise taxes were applied to alcohol. The methodology of the 2012 GSAH involved collaboration with all six WHO regional offices and national representatives nominated by member states' ministries of health. Data collection was also conducted in conjunction with the European Commission for EU countries. The survey questionnaire, prepared in multiple languages, addressed alcohol policy, consumption, and health indicators. Some countries prohibit the production and/or consumption of alcohol, often for religious reasons. For example, 9% of surveyed countries had laws banning alcohol production or consumption, with Islam being the predominant religion in these regions. In countries where alcohol consumption is not banned, taxation methods vary widely. For instance, 11 countries did not tax beer, 28 did not tax wine, and 15 did not tax spirits. Historical reasons often explain the absence of alcohol taxation in some countries. Globally, alcohol excise taxation methods include ad valorem taxation, specific taxation, unitary taxation, and combinations of these methods. The 2012 GSAH reported that 46 countries used ad valorem taxation only, 24 used specific taxation only, five used unitary taxation only, and 63 used two or more taxation systems. However, 38 of these 63 countries did not provide information on the specific methods used. Some countries calculate the tax due on alcoholic beverages as the sum of two or more taxation systems, while others use the higher of two or more systems. Unrecorded alcohol consumption poses challenges for taxation. It reduces the effectiveness of tax increases on alcohol consumption, as higher prices for recorded alcohol may lead to substitution with unrecorded alcohol. Additionally, excise taxes are not applied to unrecorded alcohol, resulting in lost tax revenue. The implementation of taxation and pricing policies involves addressing issues such as tax administration, substitution effects, affordability, tax rate determination, tax avoidance and evasion, protection of domestic brands, and the impact of taxation on the poor. It also requires consideration of trade agreements, the general economy, and other alcohol control policies. Earmarked taxation, where tax revenues are allocated to specific purposes, is another important aspect of alcohol taxation policy.
